title: The Rented House in Labone Where Ashesi University Began
dek: A Microsoft engineer who became a father left Seattle to build a university in Ghana, and when the money for a campus fell short he opened in a converted house.

story.event: Leaving Microsoft to found a university, and opening it in a rented house in Accra
story.summary: Patrick Awuah, a Ghanaian engineer at Microsoft in Seattle, decided after becoming a father to return to Africa, and in 1997 gave up his software career to found a university that would teach critical thinking and ethics instead of rote learning. After a feasibility study at Berkeley and a US foundation set up in 1999, plans to build a campus first fell through, so Ashesi opened in 2002 in a rented house in Labone, Accra, with about thirty students. It survived accreditation troubles and a year it barely made payroll, covered its operating costs from 2008 and moved to its own campus at Berekuso in 2011.
paragraphs: In the mid-1990s Patrick Awuah was an engineer at Microsoft in Seattle, several years into what became an eight-year career there. He had left Ghana on a scholarship to Swarthmore College, where teachers wanted him to think rather than memorise, and being part of a team designing new software was, he later said, "brilliant." Then he became a father. "For the first time, Africa mattered more to me than ever before," he told a TED audience in 2007.

What he could see of the continent was bleak. Somalia had collapsed and Rwanda was in the throes of genocide, he recalled: "I couldn't just stay in Seattle and raise my kids in an upper-middle class neighborhood and feel good about it." Back in Ghana to ask what was wrong, he kept hearing about corruption, weak institutions and the leaders who ran them. He first assumed he would start a software firm, Graphic Business later reported, until he saw how hard it would be to find well-trained engineers at home. The universities, he concluded, taught by rote, with little emphasis on ethics.

In 1997 he gave up his software career. At the University of California, Berkeley, where he took an MBA, he and classmates including Nina Marini studied in 1998 whether a private university in Ghana could work, and in 1999 the two set up the Ashesi University Foundation in Seattle. The plan was to raise money and build a campus first. That fell through when a downturn in the United States made fundraising harder, the university later recorded, so in 2002 Ashesi, Akan for "beginning", opened in a rented house in Labone, Accra, converted into classrooms, with a first class of about thirty students.

A month into classes, a student emailed him: "I am thinking now." The early years were not smooth; Graphic Business reports run-ins with the National Accreditation Board and a year when Ashesi barely made payroll. By mid-2007 two classes had graduated and, Awuah said, every graduate had been placed in work. In 2008 fees from students who could afford them covered operating costs for the first time, and in 2011 Ashesi moved to its own campus at Berekuso, overlooking Accra.

quote.text: We must make it our own.  We are in this very like him, who having need of fire, went to a neighbour's house to fetch it, and finding a very good one there, sat down to warm himself without remembering to carry any with him home.
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne mocks the man who warms himself at a neighbour's fire and forgets to carry any home. Awuah had sat by a very good fire at Swarthmore and Microsoft; Ashesi was his attempt to carry it back, and to teach students to make what they learn their own.

reflection: Awuah's plan had a proper campus in it. When the money would not come in time, he did not wait for it; he rented a house and began with the students he had. The thing that mattered, a different way of teaching, did not need the buildings to start.

You probably carry something you learned elsewhere, from a teacher, a training course or a place that worked well, that you have been meaning to bring into your own work or home. It need not arrive whole. A converted house and thirty students, or one conversation, can be how it begins.
invitation: Name one good practice you once saw somewhere else and admired. Today, describe it to one colleague or family member, and ask together what the smallest version of it here would look like.

research_notes: First class: Ashesi, Berkeley Haas and Times Higher Education say 30 students; Graphic Business (2017) says 27, nearly half on scholarship; Ashesi's 2012 community report says 30 admitted from 150 applicants. The story says 'about thirty'. Money raised before opening: Berkeley Haas says $2.5 million; Ashesi's 2012 community report says $3.3 million; the story gives no figure. Opening month: Ashesi's 2018 timeline says May 2002, while another Ashesi page found in search (now offline) gave 4 March 2002; the story says only 2002. First graduation: 2005 on Ashesi's history page and in Berkeley Haas, 2006 in the 2012 community report; the story uses Awuah's own June 2007 statement that two classes had graduated and all were placed. Microsoft tenure: Graphic Business says eight years; Ashesi dates his departure to 1997. The software-firm idea comes only from Graphic Business and is attributed. The 'downturn' reason for opening in a rented house is Ashesi's own account. Ashesi's history page links its name to lines it attributes to Goethe; that attribution is doubtful and the lines are not used. The TED quotations keep Awuah's American spelling ('neighborhood'). Ashesi's own pages are cited from Wayback Machine copies because the live pages have moved. The Montaigne passage is about digesting learning rather than borrowing it; the fire image is applied to Awuah by analogy.
